summary: Patch the management plane and the PHP layer first: Palo Alto Networks now says its PAN-OS management interface was exploited through a path that starts with PHP2Shell, the flaw set used against Check Point gateways earlier this month, while Check Point management servers (GT13), vCenter and SAP NetWeaver stay on the exploited list. New since yesterday: Hex.pm and Microsoft Entra Connect Health are confirmed as exploited services; Broadcom fixed 23 VMware flaws; a run of US federal intrusions (CIA, NGA and ODNI open-source system, FinCEN) are close in time but not linked by any source; ARTEX agent tooling turned up in Belgian and Hugging Face cases; Douzone Bizon's backup service adds victims in Korea next to the PLAID KARTE notices in Japan; Korean savings banks keep reporting hacks; and the DOJ moved to forfeit over $1.1 billion from the Binance theft. Grouping by attribute is labelled as inference; timing alone is never a cause.

patterns.title: Exploited now: PAN-OS management via PHP2Shell and Fragnesia, Check Point management servers, vCenter, Hex.pm, Entra Connect Health, Vite dev servers
patterns.narrative: Exploitation is stated by a vendor, agency or the victim for each item here. New on Nov 24: Palo Alto Networks bulletin PAN-SA-2026-0015 says the Linux kernel privilege-escalation flaw Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300) was exploited against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet, and that the only known path first requires PHP2Shell, the PHP flaw set Check Point says was chained to root unpatched gateways from Oct 30. Hex says an attacker used CVE-2026-129514 on Nov 23 to run commands on hex.pm web servers and could have read password hashes, API key hashes and 2FA secrets. Microsoft says a flaw in the Entra Connect Health API gave read-only access to tenant metadata (tenant IDs, domains, technical contacts) from July until a fix on Nov 19. HoneyLabs saw exploit attempts against exposed Vite dev servers from Nov 15 hunting for .env files and cloud keys. Still open from earlier in the week: GreyNoise's GT13 campaign against Check Point Security Management Servers, Google's report of ARMORY CASTLE exploiting a vCenter authentication bypass as a zero-day, CISA's KEV entry for SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-42884, GL.iNet's abused cloud management, and Amazon's account of AI agents exploiting a MONAI Label zero-day. The common thread is management and developer-facing surfaces: interfaces that should not be reachable from the internet at all.
patterns.caveat: Each exploitation claim concerns one product and different attackers; grouping them is by attribute, not by a shared actor. Palo Alto rates its bulletin informational and names no victims or count. The two Entra Connect Health records describe one incident reported twice. HoneyLabs saw attempts on honeypots, not successful compromises. GT13's activity window ended Nov 2.

edges.rel: PAN-OS exploit path starts with the same PHP2Shell flaw
both target firewall management planes; different products, no shared actor stated

patterns.title: Patch before attacks: NGINX HTTP/2, phpAfterShell, 23 VMware flaws and a batch of unpatched ZDI 0-day advisories
patterns.narrative: Critical fixes with public detail keep landing faster than most patch cycles. CERT-FR's NGINX HTTP/2 remote code execution alert (public proof of concept for CVE-2026-123007) reaches into Synology DSM, which fixed the same CVE, and Xint chained one of the NGINX flaws with a Linux kernel bug for root. phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714) bypasses the October PHP2Shell fixes, and HKCERT lists the same CVE in F5 BIG-IP; that matters more now that Palo Alto says PHP2Shell is the first step in exploiting PAN-OS. On Nov 24 Broadcom's VMSA-2026-0011 fixed 23 VMware flaws, including a vCenter directory-service authentication bypass (CVE-2026-123903), in the same week Google reported a different vCenter bypass exploited as a zero-day. ZDI published 0-day advisories with no vendor fix for GNU Inetutils ftp, BusyBox ftpd, PyTorch file loading, pip and LiteLLM. SolarWinds Serv-U, Chrome 158, Adobe (113 flaws), Thunderbird, Joomla, Roundcube, WHMCS, nginx early-data, runc and Flatpak fixes also landed. OpenSSL rated its QUIC flaw Low and schedules fixes for Dec 1.
patterns.caveat: Most items have no reported exploitation; this pattern ranks urgency from vendor and agency ratings and public exploit code, not from attacks seen. The two vCenter flaws are different CVEs. ZDI 0-day advisories mean no fix was available at publication, not that attacks are happening.

edges.rel: chained to kernel bug for root (Xint)
same CVE-2026-123007, fixed in Synology DSM
same flaw CVE-2026-126714 in F5 BIG-IP (HKCERT)

patterns.title: One platform, many victims: PLAID KARTE notices keep coming in Japan, and Douzone Bizon's backup service adds victims in Korea
patterns.narrative: PLAID says a vulnerability in its KARTE customer-experience platform was exploited on Nov 13; since then customer companies have published their own counts, each saying the data was taken from KARTE, not their own systems. ZOZO (about 15.18 million), SMBC (up to about 14 million) and Marui Group (about 8.8 million) are the largest, with DHC, MUFG Bank, Sharp, Mainichi, Canon Marketing Japan, Suntory Wellness, Timee and others behind them; on Nov 24 Kaunet's second report put its count at 300,525 records after removing duplicates. In Korea a smaller cascade runs through Douzone Bizon's outsourced APO backup service: the Damyang County Cultural Foundation said on Nov 20 that data may have leaked through a breach of Douzone backup servers, and on Nov 23 Boannews listed Genesis Lab and Incheon Airport Facilities Management as further Douzone clients told their backup data may have been taken. For defenders the lesson is the same in both: a single SaaS or backup supplier holds copies of many customers' data, and notices arrive one customer at a time over weeks.
patterns.caveat: KARTE links are stated by each customer; the Douzone victims each name Douzone's backup service, but no source on file ties the Damyang notice and the Boannews list to one intrusion, so the edge between them is an inference. Counts are each company's own and may include duplicates.

patterns.title: Breaches through a provider, not the front door: Next, Decathlon, Gatwick AutoPay, Little Vista and the n0n vendor claims
patterns.narrative: A large share of this week's confirmed breaches happened at a supplier. Next told investors an external technology supplier had a cyber incident with access to data linked to Next; Decathlon confirmed malicious access to customer data at an external service provider; Gatwick disabled AutoPay after unauthorised access to that third-party parking payment system; Dublin childcare software firm Little Vista told crèches that children's and parents' data could be accessed. Earlier in the week JPMorgan said vendors that serve it were hit, Samsung named a third-party provider for its North American TV business, MoEngage reported access to its cloud, Carnegie's donation vendor and Phoebe's former vendor sent notices, and CloudSEK described a logistics portal reached with stealer-log credentials from a vendor's machine. The defender's action is the same each time: know which suppliers hold your customer data, and what they would tell you and when.
patterns.caveat: These are grouped because each victim names a provider; the providers are different and no shared attacker is stated. The n0n group name appears in claims about JPMorgan- and Samsung-related vendors, which is a claim, not a confirmed link. Next says customer personal data was not compromised.

edges.rel: same group name (n0n) in both claims; separate victims, no shared supplier stated
both hospitality booking platforms; different providers
both retailers name an external provider; different providers

patterns.title: AI-run intrusions: ARTEX shows up in a Belgian incident and on Hugging Face, CyberStrikeAI in a cloud breach, and agencies warn
patterns.narrative: Agent frameworks are now in incident reports, not only in research. NVISO says the LLM tool ARTEX deployed the ZQAgent Linux backdoor in a Belgian incident (with similar samples from Taiwan), tied to a cluster it calls FOG0003; JFrog says with high confidence that malicious Hugging Face models which stole host secrets were created inside an ARTEX agent task and leaked their own operator. Wiz counts a sharp rise in successful ARTEX-style attacks and describes a CyberStrikeAI-run intrusion that reached 3,392 users' sessions across seven EKS clusters. Amazon says Cairn-driven agents exploited a MONAI Label zero-day within minutes. Agencies are responding: Italy's ACN and CSIRT Italia, Canada's Cyber Centre, NZ's NCSC and the UK NCSC all warned in the last week, the UK NCSC's point being that the agents exploit familiar weaknesses, faster. On the other side, malware is using models too (F6's RatHat Android trojan uses Gemini) and Fortinet describes 'Godzilla AI', a marketplace for malicious tooling.
patterns.caveat: ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI are open-source tools used by different operators; sharing a tool is not sharing an actor, and no source links the Belgian, Hugging Face and Wiz cases to one operator. Vendor counts of 'AI-driven' attacks depend on each vendor's attribution method.

edges.rel: same Wiz post
same tool (ARTEX) named; no shared operator stated
EU Academy user data leaked in the same Commission attack (Euronews)

patterns.title: Developers as the way in: fake Ollama and Claude installers, poisoned models and packages, and package-registry compromise
patterns.narrative: Attackers keep going after the people and tools that build software. AhnLab says a Korean-language fake Ollama site installs real Ollama alongside WinWyvern, which uses a signed driver (BYOVD) to blind local antivirus; Vietnamese media relayed the same finding on Nov 24. A fake 'Claude Opus 5 Free Desktop' app spreads RevStealer, and Cato saw Google ads for fake Codex, Claude Code and Homebrew installers on macOS. Socket found 13 malicious NuGet packages posing as job-interview tests; JFrog found poisoned Hugging Face models; Hex.pm's web servers were breached (no changed packages found); NoMachine says a Windows installer was compromised; Wordfence held backdoored releases of WP plugins; a study of LLM API routers found some inject malicious code. Apiiro reports Claude Code 'don't ask again' approvals leaving secrets in public repositories, and eSentire saw Vinci RAT delivered through a Microsoft Store app.
patterns.caveat: Different actors and techniques; the grouping is by target (developers and their tools), not by campaign. The two fake-Ollama records describe the same AhnLab finding.

edges.rel: same AhnLab finding on fake Ollama installer (VTV)
both pose as AI coding/assistant installers; different malware and platforms

patterns.title: Access through people: help-desk vishing that defeats MFA, device-code phishing, and Black Friday lures
patterns.narrative: Most initial access described this week needed no exploit. Palo Alto Networks researchers say two clusters it calls Vortex and Cinder phoned staff as IT support: Vortex registered its own MFA device after an adversary-in-the-middle login, Cinder reused a persistent session token so no new Duo prompt appeared, and both stole Microsoft 365 data and demanded payment. ReversingLabs ties SSO vishing to a new extortion group, Inception, and Unit 42 describes Com-affiliated vishing. VMRay says EvilTokens phishing hosts kept appearing after Microsoft's September takedown, now on Bunny CDN. Device-code phishing appears with SharePoint lures (Hornetsecurity) and Black Friday lures (Cofense). The shopping season brings fake shops (CloudSEK: 4,660 domains), fake deals (Doppel), fake delivery notices (FortiGuard), brand giveaways (Spar) and fake recall SMS (Porsche China); police in Styria and Austria warn of phishing using data from tourism-sector leaks, and Israel's INCD of fake police traffic-fine SMS.
patterns.caveat: Shared techniques, not a shared actor: no source links Vortex, Cinder, Inception and Com. Two records each describe the Unit 42 Vortex/Cinder research and the Austrian tourism-data warnings. Seasonal volume figures come from vendors with different methods.

edges.rel: same research team and technique (IT-support vishing); clusters named differently, no link stated
same technique (SSO vishing); no shared actor stated
same technique (device-code phishing), different lures

patterns.title: US federal intrusions in one week: CIA, NGA and ODNI open-source system, FinCEN, FBI's NCIC, USDA
patterns.narrative: Within six days several US federal bodies reported or were reported to have intrusions. The New York Times reported (relayed by Reuters and others) that the CIA and ODNI, and per later reports the NGA, found an intrusion into an open-source intelligence analysis system that exposed some unclassified information; ODNI says classified systems and critical capabilities were not affected, and two Times sources said early indicators point to China, though investigators do not yet know who is responsible. On Nov 24 FinCEN said it is investigating unauthorized access to a limited part of its systems and took some offline. Before that, the FBI was reported to be investigating an apparent breach of its NCIC criminal database (Nov 20) and USDA took systems offline after an internal incident (Nov 19). Defenders in government and their contractors should treat each as a prompt to check exposure, not as one campaign.
patterns.caveat: Only timing connects these. No source states a common actor or method; the China indication applies only to the CIA/ODNI case and comes from unnamed sources. Several records describe the CIA/ODNI story from different outlets and are likely duplicates.

edges.rel: days apart; no stated link
reported the same week; no stated link

patterns.title: State pressure on Europe and the Middle East: a new Iran-nexus espionage group, Albania's warning, tanker attacks, and UK alerts on Russian sabotage
patterns.narrative: Check Point describes Volant Manticore, a previously undocumented Iran-nexus espionage group (high confidence on Iran, medium on an MOIS link) that sent a fake CV with the KuboShell backdoor to a Cyprus-based airline and from September 2026 healthcare-themed lures to Saudi organisations. Albania's State Security Agency chief says Iranian operations against Albania continue into 2026 as smaller, more frequent data theft and leak operations with pressure via Telegram. The US is investigating whether Iran was behind attacks on up to 50 energy tankers, with Russia also considered and no direct evidence found yet. In the UK, the NPSA and Ministry of Defence alerted firms supplying Ukraine's forces to increased Russian sabotage attempts via proxies, and the government briefed defence and infrastructure chief executives on Russian threats including cyber attacks. NoName057(16) put a Belgian DDoS researcher on its blacklist; Seqrite reported phishing of Ukrainian government bodies.
patterns.caveat: Each item names one state at most and these are separate operations; grouping them by region is our inference. Tanker attribution is under investigation, not established. Israel Police's shutdown of internal systems this week has no stated cause and is not included as state activity.

edges.rel: same UK warning on Russian threats to defence suppliers, reported from two angles
both describe Iranian operations against European states; different targets, no link stated

patterns.title: South Korea: savings-bank hacks keep coming while regulators move hacking liability onto firms
patterns.narrative: Hankyung counts five savings banks (Yegaram, Welcome, DB, OK and Hana) hacked since late September; Hana says its mobile customer re-verification system was breached on Nov 16 (552 customers), and on Nov 25 Korea Investment Savings Bank said abnormal external transactions on its mobile homepage overnight on Nov 22-23 leaked data of about 86,000 customers. Payment processors KICC and Welcome Payments and Samsung Securities also reported leaks this week. Policy is moving in the same direction: the FSC's draft digital asset act would make exchanges liable without fault for hacking losses and set revenue-based penalties, lawmakers have not yet settled a revenue-based fine in the electronic financial transactions amendment, the FTC asked banks to fix 73 unfair terms on hacking liability, the FSC fined Lotte Card for under-disclosing hacking risk, regulators ran a joint crisis drill with major banks, and the science ministry counts intrusions up 31 percent.
patterns.caveat: No source links the savings-bank intrusions to one actor or one flaw; they hit different systems. The policy moves are not stated to respond to any particular hack. Several FSC draft-law records are the same announcement from different outlets.

patterns.title: Binance theft: freezing order, coinjoin laundering, and a US forfeiture action for over $1.1 billion; smaller bridges and vaults drained
patterns.narrative: The Oct 29 Binance theft is moving through recovery and laundering at once. Binance won a $6.5 billion worldwide freezing order from the ADGM Courts (Nov 18); Lookonchain saw the thief move another 137,602 ETH on Nov 19; Elliptic traced at least 3,930 BTC into coinjoins across thousands of wallets; and on Nov 23 the US Justice Department filed a civil action to forfeit over $1.1 billion in USDC it says are proceeds of the theft by North Korean cyber actors. Smaller thefts continued: Chainflip vaults drained, the CYBER bridge's validator key taken, unbacked tokens minted on the Fusionist ACE bridge, Wagyu's XMR1 deployer drained and Malaysian exchange SINEGY's hot wallet breached. For exchanges and bridges, signing-key custody remains the single point of failure.
patterns.caveat: The Binance records are one theft, linked by the sources named; North Korean attribution is the DOJ's. The smaller thefts are grouped by sector only, with no shared attacker stated.

edges.rel: same Oct 29 Binance theft; thief moves more ETH for laundering

patterns.title: Energy and industry: fuel sales halted in Bolivia, a US steel plant subsidiary, a uranium site and a wind maker hit; tankers under attack
patterns.narrative: Operational businesses reported intrusions across the week. Bolivia's state fuel company YPFB said a breach suspended billing and fuel sales at its stations until service was restored; Kyoei Steel said its US subsidiary with a plant in El Paso was hit from Nov 17-19 with no effect on shipments so far; Peninsula Energy said an operating server at its Lance uranium project was attacked; Suzlon Energy reported a cyber incident to CERT-In. At sea, the US is investigating attacks on up to 50 energy tankers. Exposed controllers remain an open door: UK agencies are working to secure refrigeration controllers, CISA and INCIBE published Danfoss advisories (including default credentials), CERT@VDE flagged WAGO controller flaws, and a forum seller claims SCADA access to a Taiwan substation.
patterns.caveat: Grouped by sector only; these organisations were hit by different, mostly unnamed attackers, and several reports do not say whether operational technology was touched. The Taiwan substation item is an unverified sale claim.

edges.rel: energy firms reporting in the same days; no stated link
